questions.prompt: In this course's vocabulary, what is the real difference between a 'system of record' and a 'system of action'?
options: A system of record owns the authoritative copy of a given type of data; a system of action is the platform where a business process actually executes, gets approved, and gets tracked — which is usually ServiceNow's own role
A system of record is always deployed on-premises, while a system of action is always a cloud SaaS product
The two terms are interchangeable labels different vendors use for the same concept
A system of action permanently stores data, while a system of record only processes it temporarily and then discards it
A system of record is always Workday or SAP, and a system of action is always ServiceNow, regardless of the actual integration
questions.distractorExplain: Option B confuses deployment location with the actual distinction — Lesson 1 never ties either term to on-prem vs. cloud; the distinction is about who owns the authoritative data versus who runs the process, not where either system happens to be hosted.
questions.explain: Lesson 1's key-terms table draws exactly this line: a system of record owns the authoritative data (e.g., Workday for employee data), while a system of action is where the process runs, gets approved, and gets tracked (ServiceNow's typical role) — and a system of action with no integration to the real system of record can't act on data it can't see.

questions.prompt: A legacy mainframe billing system can only export a flat file once a night and cannot accept any inbound HTTP calls at all. Which integration pattern fits, and why would a Scripted REST API be the wrong tool here?
options: A scheduled Import Set, because the system can't receive an inbound HTTP call at all — a Scripted REST API needs the external system to call it, which this system is structurally unable to do
A Scripted REST API, because it is the most modern option and should always be preferred regardless of what the external system can actually do
An OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials REST Message, because every legacy system eventually needs a token-based credential
An IntegrationHub spoke, because every external system has an official spoke available
questions.explain: Lesson 2's own check-yourself scenario is exactly this: a Scripted REST API is inbound — it requires the external system to initiate an HTTP call against ServiceNow. A system that can only drop a nightly flat file and accepts no inbound calls can't do that, so the batch, file-based Import Set is the right (if less modern-looking) answer.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world scenario to the integration pattern category it belongs to.
left: Datadog detects a server outage and immediately calls ServiceNow to create an Incident, the instant it happens
A nightly CSV export from an HR system lands and is transformed into ServiceNow records through a Transform Map
A ServiceNow Change Request gets approved and ServiceNow calls out to a deployment tool to carry out the change
ServiceNow receives new Incidents from a monitoring tool and also pushes Incident status changes back out to keep that tool's dashboard current
right: Bidirectional — two separate patterns running side by side
questions.explain: Datadog's push is event-driven (triggered by something happening, not polled); the nightly HR file is a classic Import Set inbound pattern; the approved Change triggering a deployment call is outbound via REST Message; and receiving-plus-pushing-back-status is Lesson 2's bidirectional case — two simpler patterns running side by side, not one mechanism doing two things.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: to actually call a configured REST Message from a Script Include, Business Rule, or Scheduled Job, ServiceNow's real script API class is ________ (referenced as sn_ws.________ in a scoped application).
questions.explain: Lesson 6 names the real class: RESTMessageV2, referenced as sn_ws.RESTMessageV2 in a scoped application (because it lives in the Web Services Integration Suite's own scope) or directly as RESTMessageV2 in Global scope.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the real order Chapter 2 and its lab build a working outbound REST integration.
items: Configure the parent REST Message record with its base Endpoint and default Authentication Profile
Add a REST Message Function with its own HTTP method, relative path, and any needed headers or body template
Run the Function's built-in Test capability and confirm a clean response before writing any script
Call the REST Message from a Script Include using RESTMessageV2, filling placeholders with setStringParameterNoEscape() before execute()
questions.explain: Lessons 4-7 build in exactly this order: the parent REST Message's Endpoint and Authentication Profile first (since every Function inherits it), then a Function per real operation, then Test at the record level to isolate configuration problems before any script exists, and only then call it from RESTMessageV2 in script — testing first is what lets a later script failure be diagnosed as a script problem, not a configuration one.

questions.prompt: You configure a new REST Message Function, run its built-in Test, and get back a 401 status code. Which part of the configuration is the most likely problem, and why?
options: The Authentication Profile — a 401 specifically signals an authorization failure, not a wrong path (which would be 404) or a server-side error (which would be 500)
The relative path on the Function, since any configuration mistake always surfaces as a 401 regardless of its real cause
The base Endpoint on the parent REST Message, since Functions never have their own Endpoint field
Nothing in the REST Message record — a 401 always means the external system itself is down
questions.explain: Lesson 5's own check-yourself draws this line explicitly: 200 is success, 401 signals the Authentication Profile is wrong, 404 signals a bad path, and 500 signals the external system itself errored — testing at the record level isolates exactly which piece is broken before any script exists.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about calling a REST Message with RESTMessageV2, per Lesson 6.
options: setStringParameterNoEscape() must be called once per placeholder the Function's Endpoint or Content template defines, before execute() runs
.execute() throws a JavaScript exception when the network call itself can't complete — DNS failure, unreachable host, timeout — which is why it belongs inside a try/catch
A 404 or 500 returned by the external system causes .execute() to throw an exception just like a network failure would
.getBody() returns the raw response body as a string, which still needs JSON.parse() to access individual fields
RESTMessageV2 is referenced identically in every scope, with no namespace difference between scoped applications and Global
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is explicit: each placeholder needs its own setStringParameterNoEscape() call; .execute() only throws on a true network-level failure (a 404/500 still returns normally as a response object carrying that status code, it does not throw); and .getBody() returns a raw string that still needs JSON.parse(). The namespace does differ — sn_ws.RESTMessageV2 in scoped apps vs. RESTMessageV2 in Global — so that last statement is false.

questions.prompt: A scheduled ServiceNow job checks order status against a partner's API every 15 minutes, with no human user involved anywhere in the process. The partner supports both Basic Auth and OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials. Which should you configure, and what's the specific justification?
options: OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials — this is a recurring, unattended job with no human user, and Basic Auth would send the real username and password on the wire thousands of times a month with no expiration and a shared-password revocation problem
Basic Auth — it's faster to configure, and speed of initial setup is what a technical reviewer actually cares about
OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code grant — because OAuth is always more secure than Basic Auth regardless of grant type
Either one — there is no real operational difference once the connection runs over HTTPS
questions.explain: Lesson 11's authentication lab reasons through exactly this: the job is unattended with no human user, which rules out Authorization Code (reserved for a human delegating access) and favors Client Credentials; and the sheer frequency of this job makes Basic Auth's every-request credential exposure and no-expiration weaknesses a real, not hypothetical, risk.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: unlike standard HTTPS, where only the server proves its identity, mutual TLS requires both the client and the server to present and verify ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 10 defines mutual TLS as both sides presenting and verifying certificates — the TLS handshake itself fails if either certificate doesn't check out, before any REST Message script even runs.

questions.prompt: Match each authentication mechanism to the property that specifically defines it in this chapter.
right: Base64-encodes username:password into the Authorization header on every single request, with no built-in expiration
Exchanges a client ID and secret for a short-lived access token that ServiceNow caches and refreshes automatically, with no human user involved
Requires both the client and the server to present and verify certificates before the connection is even accepted
A static shared-secret string, commonly sent in a custom header like X-API-Key, with no universal spec or scope model
questions.explain: Each mechanism has one defining trait from this chapter: Basic Auth resends the real credential every request with no expiration (Lesson 8); Client Credentials is the no-human-user OAuth grant with automatic token lifecycle (Lesson 9); mutual TLS is the only one requiring certificate verification on both sides (Lesson 10); and an API key is a vendor-specific shared secret with no standardized spec (Lesson 10).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Basic Authentication, per Lesson 8.
options: Base64 encoding is reversible and is not a form of encryption — anyone intercepting the header can decode it straight back to the real username and password
Over plain HTTP (not HTTPS), a Basic Auth header is effectively exposed in plaintext to anyone positioned to see the traffic
A Basic Auth credential automatically expires after about an hour, the same as an OAuth access token
Revoking one integration's access often means changing a password shared across several other integrations, breaking them too
Basic Auth is never an acceptable choice for any real ServiceNow integration, even internally or in a sandbox
questions.explain: Lesson 8 is explicit that base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption; that plain HTTP exposes the decoded header in seconds; and that a shared service-account password creates a real revocation problem. It states the opposite of the hour-expiration claim — a Basic Auth credential has no built-in expiration at all, unlike an OAuth token — and the lesson's own honest rule still allows Basic Auth for a quick internal test or sandbox.

questions.prompt: An integration needs to combine fields from two different ServiceNow tables into one response and reject a request that's missing a required field with a custom error message. Which tool fits, and why can't the Table API do this?
options: A Scripted REST API — the Table API always returns one table's raw field structure as-is and has no way to run custom logic, combine multiple tables, or validate a payload beyond a table's own ACLs and Business Rules
The Table API with sysparm_fields set to include both tables' fields in one call
The Table API with sysparm_query set to join the two tables
Either tool works identically, since both expose the same underlying GlideRecord data
questions.explain: Lesson 12 draws this line explicitly: the Table API is automatic and zero-code, which is exactly why it can't validate beyond a table's own ACLs/Business Rules, reshape a response, or combine data from more than one table — a Scripted REST API exists specifically for the transformation, aggregation, or custom validation the Table API's convenience can't provide.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order Lesson 15's lab builds a versioned Scripted REST API for the equipment-checkout scenario.
items: Create the API definition (sys_ws_definition) with its base path and required role, checked by the platform before any Resource script runs
Create a Version record (v1) that contributes its own /v1 base-path segment
Create the Resource with its relative path /checkout/{sys_id} and a GET method
In the Resource script, call gr.get() on the path parameter and return a 404 before building any response body if it returns false
questions.explain: The lab builds top-down: the API definition and its required role first (since the platform checks that role before any script runs), then the Version that contributes the /v1 segment, then the Resource itself with its relative path and method, and only then the script logic that looks up the record and returns 404 before ever reaching response.setBody().

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Scripted REST API's required roles are evaluated by the platform ________ any Resource's script runs, so a caller without the role never even reaches the script.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 is explicit that the API-level role requirement is checked first, before any Resource's script executes — it keeps the entire API unreachable to the wrong caller rather than relying on every script to re-check gs.hasRole() correctly every time.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Table API, per Lesson 12.
options: Every table in a ServiceNow instance already has a working Table API the moment the table exists, with no sys_ws_definition record required
sysparm_query accepts the same encoded-query syntax (including ^ for AND) that GlideRecord's addQuery()/addEncodedQuery() build and consume
A list GET's response wraps its payload in a top-level result key, as an array
sysparm_fields controls which records match the query, the same way sysparm_query does
The Table API can reshape a response into a custom format an external system expects
questions.explain: Lesson 12 confirms the Table API requires zero custom scripting, uses the same encoded-query syntax on sysparm_query, and wraps list results in an array under result. sysparm_fields trims which fields appear in the response — it doesn't affect which records match, that's sysparm_query's job — and the Table API explicitly cannot reshape a response into a custom format; that's exactly what a Scripted REST API is for.

questions.prompt: Multiple teams keep hand-configuring a generic REST step to check stock in a niche internal inventory system with no official ServiceNow spoke. What's the right long-term fix, and what does it change for the teams using it afterward?
options: Build a custom action with the inventory API's REST step configured once inside it — every flow builder afterward drops the finished action in and supplies a SKU, never touching the inventory system's endpoint or Authentication Profile themselves
Ask ServiceNow to release an official spoke for this specific internal system before anyone can proceed
Have every flow builder keep configuring their own generic REST step, since that's exactly what IntegrationHub's generic REST step is designed for
Write a new Scripted REST API on the inventory system's own server to replace the REST call entirely
questions.explain: Lessons 18 and 19's whole point is this exact gap: when no official spoke exists, you build a custom action once — Inputs, an internal REST step configured with its own endpoint and Authentication Profile, and Outputs — and every other flow builder reuses the finished action without ever seeing the target system's API, the same way they'd reuse an official spoke's action.

questions.prompt: Match each IntegrationHub term to its real definition from this chapter.
right: A ServiceNow-maintained bundle of multiple independently-usable actions for one external system
One specific operation inside a Spoke, with its own named Inputs and Outputs, droppable into any flow on its own
A new, reusable action a developer builds with its own Inputs, an internal step sequence, and Outputs, when no official spoke covers a system
A Flow Designer canvas step for calling any REST API directly, configured once per flow rather than packaged for reuse
questions.explain: Lessons 16 and 17 define each term precisely: a Spoke bundles multiple Connector Actions for one system (e.g., Slack's Post Message, Create Channel, Invite User); a Connector Action is one of those bundled operations; a custom action is what you build yourself when no spoke exists (Lesson 18); and the generic REST step lives directly on one flow's own canvas, not packaged for reuse the way a custom action is.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: IntegrationHub is a separately-licensed ________, not a feature that ships free with every ServiceNow edition.
questions.explain: Lesson 16 states this directly: before designing a solution around a spoke or custom action, confirm the instance actually has an IntegrationHub entitlement, because — unlike basic Flow Designer — it's a separately-licensed add-on, the same commercial pattern as Performance Analytics.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order Lesson 19's lab designs the custom 'Check Inventory Level' action.
items: Define the action's Inputs — in this case, a single required Item SKU field
Configure the internal REST step's Endpoint, Method, and Authentication Profile against the inventory system's real API
Define the Outputs, exposing only the Quantity Available field a consumer actually needs
Sanity-check the Input names, Output scope, and Authentication Profile before publishing the action for other flow builders to use
questions.explain: Lesson 18's three-part structure — Inputs, internal step sequence, Outputs — is exactly the order Lesson 19 works through: decide what a consumer must supply, configure the real API call once inside the action, decide what a consumer gets back, and only then run the publish checklist (clear Input names, a minimal Output set, a shared rather than personal credential).

questions.prompt: An integration script gets a 404 on one call and a 503 on another. Which one should the retry logic actually retry, and why?
options: Only the 503 — a 4xx means the request itself is wrong, so retrying an identical request produces an identical failure, while a 503 may be a transient server-side problem that a later attempt can succeed past
Only the 404 — a missing resource might appear if you just try again fast enough
Both — any non-200 status is always worth retrying regardless of its specific code
Neither — any failed call should simply be logged once and never retried
questions.explain: Lessons 20 and 23 both draw this line explicitly: a timeout or a 5xx is often worth retrying because the failure may be transient, while a 4xx (bad request, bad auth, not found) means the request itself is wrong — retrying it just repeats the same failure, wasting an attempt instead of fixing anything.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 23's hardened script, response.getErrorMessage() is checked alongside the status code. What specific situation does a non-empty getErrorMessage() signal, that a status code alone cannot?
options: A transport-level failure — the host was unreachable or the connection timed out before any real HTTP response came back at all, so there is no status code to read in the first place
That the external system returned a 4xx client error
That the JSON body, while present, failed to parse
That the call succeeded with a 200 but the data was stale
questions.explain: Lesson 23 is explicit that RESTMessageV2.execute() generally doesn't throw for an HTTP-level failure — a 4xx/5xx still comes back as a normal response object with a real status code. getErrorMessage() returning non-empty is the signal for the other case: a transport-level failure where no real HTTP response ever arrived to read a status code from, which is exactly why both checks are needed together.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about exponential backoff and idempotency, per Lessons 21-23.
options: Exponential backoff doubles the wait time between each retry (e.g. 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) instead of retrying immediately or at a fixed interval
Retrying immediately in a tight loop can make an already-overloaded external system's problem worse, not better
An idempotent operation produces the same end result whether it runs once or several times, which is what makes retrying a create operation safe
The coalesce-on-external-ID pattern inserts a new record every time, regardless of whether one already exists for that external ID
gs.sleep(milliseconds) is a real server-side API used to implement the wait between retry attempts
questions.explain: Lessons 21 and 23 establish backoff's doubling delay, the overload risk of immediate retries, idempotency's same-result-either-way definition, and gs.sleep() as the real pausing API. The fourth statement describes the opposite of the coalesce pattern — it specifically checks for an existing record by external ID first and updates it instead of inserting a duplicate.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: beyond your own gs.* calls, IntegrationHub keeps its own run-by-run record of a spoke or custom action's inputs, steps, and outputs, called the ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 22 names this directly: IntegrationHub's execution log is the first place to look when a custom spoke action fails, before digging into your own script's gs.* output, because it shows exactly where in the action's step sequence the failure happened.

questions.prompt: What is a MID Server, physically and architecturally, per Lesson 24?
options: A lightweight Java application that a customer downloads and installs on their own network, which makes outbound-only connections to the ServiceNow instance to relay work
A ServiceNow-hosted cloud service that opens an inbound connection directly into the customer's firewall
A feature flag enabled on the instance, requiring no separate installation on any machine
A load balancer ServiceNow places in front of its own cloud instance
A VPN tunnel configured entirely from ServiceNow's cloud side, with nothing installed on the customer's network
A browser extension installed on an administrator's workstation that proxies API calls
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the exact opposite of the real design — a MID Server never accepts an inbound connection from ServiceNow at all; it only ever reaches outward from inside the customer's network, which is the specific detail that makes it acceptable to security teams who default to closing every inbound firewall port.
questions.explain: Lesson 24 is explicit: a MID Server is a real, lightweight Java application a customer installs on their own machine (on-prem or in their own cloud VPC) — nothing about it lives in ServiceNow's cloud, and it only ever makes outbound-only connections to ServiceNow, polling for queued work.

questions.prompt: One integration target is an on-prem Oracle HR database behind a corporate firewall with no public-facing endpoint. Another is Meridian HR, a cloud SaaS product with a documented public HTTPS API. Which one requires a MID Server, and why doesn't the other?
options: The on-prem Oracle database requires a MID Server, because ServiceNow's cloud instance has no network path to a system with no public endpoint; Meridian HR doesn't, because ServiceNow can already open an outbound connection to its public API directly
Both require a MID Server, since every outbound integration needs one regardless of whether the target has a public endpoint
Neither requires a MID Server, since REST Messages can always reach any target directly
Only Meridian HR requires a MID Server, because cloud SaaS APIs are never reachable without one
questions.explain: This is exactly the contrast Lesson 26 draws when scoping the capstone: Meridian HR is a cloud SaaS product with a public HTTPS API, so a direct REST Message works with no MID Server; if the target were instead an on-prem database with no public endpoint, per Lesson 24's whole premise, a MID Server would become mandatory to close that reachability gap.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a MID Server always makes ________-only connections to the ServiceNow instance, polling on a short interval for queued work, so the instance never has to connect inward into the customer's network.
questions.explain: Lesson 24 names this as the real security property that makes MID Servers viable: outbound-only connections mean the customer never has to open an inbound firewall port, satisfying the default 'no inbound holes' posture most security teams require.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the real order the capstone's onboarding integration executes for one new hire.
items: Meridian HR's webhook fires, carrying only a thin payload — an employee ID and an event type
ServiceNow's Scripted REST API resource receives the webhook and reads the employeeId from the payload
OnboardingSync pulls the full employee record from Meridian HR's REST API, retrying with exponential backoff on a 5xx or transport failure
Before creating a sys_user, the script checks for an existing record by u_meridian_employee_id to avoid a duplicate
A pending sys_user and its onboarding tasks are created from the pulled, verified employee record
questions.explain: Lessons 26-28 build this exact chain: the webhook is deliberately thin (just an ID), the Scripted REST API resource reads that ID, the REST Message pull (with retries) fetches the authoritative record from Meridian HR (the real source of truth), the idempotency check runs before any insert, and only then are the sys_user and onboarding tasks actually created.

questions.prompt: Match each of the capstone's test plan cases to what it actually proves.
left: Duplicate employee ID (the same webhook redelivered twice)
right: Retries actually fire with increasing delay, then fail cleanly with one gs.error() and no partial record
Idempotency actually holds — exactly one sys_user exists afterward, with the second call logged as a skip
A bad payload is caught and logged rather than trusted, instead of producing a garbage sys_user
RESTMessageV2 requests a fresh token automatically with no code change and no manual re-authentication
questions.explain: Lesson 29's test plan ties each case to a specific earlier lesson's claim: the unreachable case proves Lesson 28's retry logic actually degrades cleanly; the duplicate case proves the u_meridian_employee_id idempotency check actually holds, not just assumed; the malformed-response case proves the failure is caught rather than trusted; and the expired-token case proves the OAuth Entity Profile's automatic refresh from Lesson 27 really works unattended.

questions.prompt: Why does the capstone's inbound webhook from Meridian HR carry only an employee ID and an event type, instead of the full new-hire record, and what does ServiceNow do immediately after receiving that thin payload?
options: Because Meridian HR, not the webhook payload, is the source of truth for the employee's real data — ServiceNow immediately calls back out to Meridian HR's own REST API to pull the authoritative full record rather than trusting whatever happened to be included in the webhook call
Because ServiceNow's Scripted REST API resource cannot accept a payload larger than a single ID field
Because Meridian HR's webhook format has no way to include more than one field per call
Because pulling the full record separately is required to avoid needing any authentication on the webhook itself
questions.explain: Lesson 26 is explicit about this design choice: a webhook payload is data in transit, not the source of truth, so trusting it blindly would make ServiceNow's picture of a new hire depend on whatever Meridian happened to include in one HTTP call. The thin notification plus a separate authoritative pull (Lesson 27) keeps Meridian HR as the single source of truth.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the design decisions behind the capstone's Meridian HR onboarding integration.
options: The pull from Meridian HR uses OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials grant because the call is server-to-server with no human user delegating access
No MID Server is needed for the Meridian HR pull because Meridian HR is a cloud SaaS product with a public HTTPS API that ServiceNow's cloud instance can already reach directly
The u_meridian_employee_id field is what lets the idempotency check recognize a redelivered webhook as already processed, instead of creating a second sys_user
The retry loop around the Meridian HR pull retries on a 4xx status the same way it retries on a 5xx, since both are equally likely to succeed on a later attempt
The webhook-receiving resource is built as a Scripted REST API, the same inbound mechanism covered in Chapter 4
questions.explain: Lessons 27-28 confirm Client Credentials fits because no human user is involved, no MID Server is needed since Meridian HR has a public endpoint, and u_meridian_employee_id is the coalesce field behind the idempotency check; the webhook resource is indeed a Scripted REST API (Lesson 26/27). The retry loop explicitly does NOT retry on a 4xx — Lesson 28 is clear that a 4xx means the request itself is wrong and retrying it three times just repeats the same failure.
